extracted.intended_audience: journalists, news editors, media analysts, and journalism scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the Discourse of News Values (DNVA) framework to evaluate or produce news stories and images by identifying nine news values and their linguistic/visual constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: The relevance of an event in relation to the current moment (recent, ongoing, seasonal, anniversary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linguistic indicators include words/phrases like "today," "now," "yesterday," and tense markers. Emphasize recency, ongoing status, or links to current dates/anniversaries to increase perceived newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: The compatibility of an event with stereotypes that audiences hold about the people, places, things, etc. involved (fits expectations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructed using stock phrases and references to recurring story types; aligns events with culturally available narratives and expectations so they 'fit' audience schemas. Use recognizable frames/themes to increase consonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: The negative aspects of an event (death, damage, conflict, scandal, crisis, loss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signalled by words such as "tragedy," "disaster," "crisis." Highlight harms, losses, conflicts, scandals or risks; negative framing increases news value through threat/harm salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The effects or consequences of an event (causal, ripple effects, predictions of effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed via causal verbs and explicit references to consequences; discuss who/what is affected, magnitude of effects, and downstream/ripple effects to demonstrate significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: The geographical or cultural nearness of an event to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked by place names, words like "here," and cultural references. Emphasize geographic closeness or cultural relevance to the target audience (local, national, diasporic ties) to raise newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: The unexpected, unusual, or surprising aspects of an event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signalled by lexical choices such as "first," "shocking," "surprise." Emphasize novelty, deviation from norms, rarity or surprise elements to increase attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superlativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The maximized or intensified aspects of an event (scope, scale, intensity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructed with intensifiers and extreme descriptors (e.g. "massive," "unprecedented"). Use comparative and superlative language to emphasize scale, degree or exceptional status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: The personal or 'human' face of an event (named individuals, ordinary people quoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signalled by names, emotion words and quotations from ordinary people. Use human faces, personal stories, and direct quotes to make abstract events vivid and relatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliteness
rubrics_metrics.description: The high status of the people, organizations, or nations involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked by titles and role labels (e.g. CEO, president). Reference elite actors, institutions or nations to increase perceived importance and authority of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic indicators for each value (aggregated)
rubrics_metrics.description: The DNVA framework maps each news value onto specific linguistic resources used to construct newsworthiness in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregated indicators as given in the framework: Negativity — words like "tragedy," "disaster," "crisis"; Timeliness — "today," "now," "yesterday," tense markers; Proximity — place names, "here," cultural references; Superlativeness — intensifiers ("massive," "unprecedented"); Eliteness — titles, role labels (CEO, president); Impact — causal verbs, references to consequences; Unexpectedness — "first," "shocking," "surprise"; Personalisation — names, emotion words, quotations from ordinary people; Consonance — stock phrases, reference to recurring story types. Use these lexical and grammatical cues when coding or composing news to make particular values salient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual Construction (photography)
rubrics_metrics.description: How news values are constructed in photographs and visual material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add an aesthetic dimension when analyzing photographs: consider composition, color, framing and capturing a dramatic moment. Visual features can instantiate the same values (e.g. proximity via location cues, personalization via faces, superlativeness via scale in the image).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical perspectives: Cognitive vs Discursive
rubrics_metrics.description: Two complementary perspectives for understanding news values: cognitive (values as criteria journalists apply) and discursive (values as constructed properties expressed in/through text/image).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both perspectives in analysis or practice: treat values both as heuristics journalists deploy in decision-making (cognitive) and as resources that are rhetorically constructed in language and visuals (discursive). This informs both content selection and micro-level textual/visual choices.
